utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case Number IT-00-41-PT, The Prosecutor versus Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ljubicic, can you hear me? You may remain seated. No need to stand up. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, let us have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Judge El Mahdi. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me is Mr. Hasan Younis who is the case manager. And good afternoon, Mr. Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Yes, for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Tomislav Jonjic, representing Mr. Ljubicic in this case. Good afternoon to my colleague Mr. Harmon as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jonjic. This session today is dedicated to a number of issues that are pending at the moment. I have been notified of the correspondence regarding the documents that have been sought by the Defence. I'm now speaking in general terms because we are sitting now in public. If there's any need to deal with the issues that would warrant a private session, would the parties please let me know of that in order to avoid any misunderstanding. Having said that, I think that the Defence has asked for access to a number of documents from two states concerned, and I would like to be sure that what I was able to conclude on the basis of the correspondence that I have seen regarding the states in question and the Defence, that we are progressing in the right direction, that the Defence does not have any major objection, and that the Defence is satisfied, if not fully, but then at least to the extent that they do not feel that they have been handicapped as far as the rights of the Defence are concerned. I should like to hear a confirmation of this from Mr. Jonjic because I think it is our mission, a mission of all of us, to ensure that the rights of the Defence are fully and completely protected. So Mr. Jonjic, I'm giving you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think it would be the most reasonable approach to start with the issue of disclosure by Bosnia and Herzegovina, since this request of the Defence was submitted earlier, chronologically speaking. The government of BH, as it is clear from the correspondence and the submissions that have been transmitted to the Chamber, handed over to the Defence on two occasions a couple of hundred documents. However, since this did not cover everything that was the subject of the request, we had to communicate on several occasions also with the mediation of the Chamber with a view of obtaining the remainder of the documents. A little more than a month ago, the government of the federation through the mediation of the Croatian liaison officer in The Hague informed the Defence that they were able to inspect the central archives of the BH Army with the objective of locating the documents which were subject of the order, but that have not been in the meantime handed over to the Defence. This permission of the government therefore concerns only the documents described in the binding order, not documents generally speaking. We are not talking about a general access to the archives of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you. I'm referring to the letter dated 13th of April. Are you aware of that letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having received this information from the Croatian liaison officer, our investigator, pro bono investigator, Mr. Goran Sijlic [phoen] on the 1st of April this year paid a visit to the BH army central archives. And on that occasion, he was given access to a certain number of documents referred to in the binding order. In view of the fact that the list of these documents is contained in the confidential part of our submission, actually, in the confidential part of the binding decision, I do not wish to identify now which particular documents were given to the investigator. All the more so because we informed thereon the Trial Chamber on the 16th of April. The individual who accompanied the investigator who was supposed to provide him assistance and who was familiar with the way the central archives of the BH army functions informed him, the investigator, that is, on that occasion that so far as other documents are concerned, other documents from the binding order which had not been handed over, the government of the Federation of BH does not have such documents at all. In other words, the assistant, the person who assisted the investigator, declared on that occasion that part of the documents that we have not yet received can probably be found at the Office of the Prosecutor. As for the remainder, it is quite possible that such documents do not exist at all; namely, that they have either been destroyed or lost. Since we cannot in any way verify the accuracy of the statements made by this employee of the BH army archives, at the 65 ter meeting held two days ago, we discussed possible ways for the Defence to obtain those documents as well. So we agreed in principle that a meeting would be held, a meeting of the representatives of the Defence and the Prosecution with a view of facilitating for the Defence an inspection of the database that the OTP has kindly provided to the Defence in an electronic form, which database, however, is so extensive, without help of the OTP, it would be impossible for us to go through the exercise. Since at the moment we don't know what the results of this cooperation with the OTP will be, in my capacity as Defence counsel of Mr. Ljubicic, at the 65 ter meeting held two days ago, I stated, fully aware, of course, of the potential consequences of my words, that if it turns out that certain documents remain missing, that fact is not going to be used by the Defence for either some kind of alibi or excuse to postpone the beginning of the trial. We're fully aware of the fact that the trial date is decided upon by the President of the Tribunal. However, since we are faced with the fact that Mr. Ljubicic is -- has been in detention for more than 29 months, we are prepared to make a sacrifice. And should such a decision be reached by the President of the Tribunal, we are ready to go on trial without waiting for the documents that are still pending and that the Government of the BH still has to hand over pursuant to the binding order. Your Honour, that would be the situation as regards the compliance of the government of BH with the binding order. I may now move on to the problems regarding the communication with the Government of the BH. But if you have questions, I'll be pleased to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I think I would like to hear the Prosecution first of all so that we can reach a satisfying conclusion for both parties. However, before I do that, let me make a remark. You say, at least this is the interpretation that I have received, that you will be prepared to make a sacrifice as Defence counsel in view of the fact that the trial date has been set in this case. This worries me a little. I'm not very happy with the -- with your impression. There should not be any sacrifice in justice, which we all have to respect here. And I think that everybody has to act in such a manner so that the final imperative, the truth, can be achieved. I had to make this remark. I felt it necessary. So before I give the floor to Mr. Harmon, I would like to hear you once again on the issue that I just raised. And after that, I will turn to Mr. Harmon, who I would like to tell us about the possibilities of helping the Defence in their research. Because it seems to me -- I understand that it is a very difficult task for them. The Defence at the same time, if I understand correctly, appreciates your kind gesture in allowing them to inspect your databases and your documents. However, if this task is left to the Defence only, it seems that the exercise is going to be time-consuming. So I should like to hear you on this, Mr. Harmon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have provided to the Defence on the 18th of September 2003 the entire collection of documents that we had seized from the Army and the Presidency of BiH. And that archives of ours that we submitted to the Defence was provided on a CD, a searchable CD. The Defence was also provided with a search engine. And this is the kind of an engine that can facilitate going through this large volume -- large set of documents to find what they may be looking for. So what we seized, in particular, the Defence has on CD-ROM. And they can do that work quite easily with the available tools. If Mr. Jonjic would like to contact me, and we have a good relationship, if he would like to contact me and identify any problem that exists in respect of this search engine that we have provided for him, we can see if there's a defect in that search engine. It seems to me, one, that given these documents were provided in September of 2003, there has been a lot of time to take a look at the documents that we have given to them. Two, if there are a select number of documents that Mr. Jonjic will identify with specificity, perhaps I can call upon my staff to search for them. But what I would like to hear from Mr. Jonjic is that documents that we have already given them have been searched by them. You know, we have our own work to do. And while I'm willing to cooperate and appreciate the cooperation that Mr. Jonjic has made in respect of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I am willing to reciprocate to some extent. Indeed, finally with these documents in hand, Mr. Jonjic should be able to find in the collection that we have given him the documents that he's looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I have no doubts whatsoever, judging by your professional qualities, that you are going to offer your assistance as much as possible to the Defence. And I am grateful to you, and I invite you to get in touch in order to clarify the matter. My concern, however, I have to admit to you, is that I feel that maybe Mr. Jonjic is in a situation which might be regarded as critical. He may have encountered some difficulties in order to find his bearings in the pile of documents. I'm very happy and I'm very grateful to the Prosecution for offering their assistance as much as possible, that is, to the Defence. And I believe that by getting in touch, by cooperating, we will arrive at the satisfying conclusions that will serve justice at the end of the day. And for that reason, Mr. Harmon, I would like to thank you. I believe, Mr. Jonjic, that you have heard what the -- what Mr. Harmon has told us. And I believe that with the assistance of the other party, with your mutual cooperation, that you will arrive at an agreeable solution. If there is no possibility to search, then we cannot be sure that we will not find what we are looking for. However, the search has to be done and it may prove to be useful. Therefore, I invite you to continue cooperating with the Prosecution and make the most of this generous offer that they have made to you. Let's go back to the other issue which has to do with the documents that have been requested from the Government of Croatia. Is there anything that you wish to add to what you have submitted to the Chamber in writing? What is the current situation with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me, I would like to go back to the issue of documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is no doubt that Mr. Harmon is right when he says that the Prosecution on the 18th of September 2003 disclosed to the Defence in an electronic form an ample number of documents originating from the BiH army and together with that a search engine for searching those documents. This part of the exercise the Defence has already completed. We have reviewed those documents. However, we're still missing a certain number of documents which may be in the, so to speak, general database, which is accessible to all the Defence counsel. And the only issue that we have discussed - that was two days ago at the 65 ter meeting - was whether there was any technical possibility for the Prosecution to facilitate our search of this extensive database which is not exclusively linked with this case, but it is a general database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, there are -- they are snowed under their work, but they could maybe try and find the means to help the Defence. Is that the gist of your request as much as it is possible? So on this base, we may expect to arrive at concrete solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly, Your Honour. And this is what I wanted to thank Mr. Harmon for. The second thing that you've mentioned the is the sacrifice on the part of the Defence. The term has been interpreted correctly, and I take full responsibility for using this term, rather than blaming the interpreters. It may have been an awkward term to use. But what I wanted to say is as following: We are absolutely aware that there is a serious risk that some of the documents that we have requested and that this decision of the Trial Chamber refers to will never be located, will never be found. And being fully aware of that, we do not wish to dwell upon this issue and waste the Tribunal's precious time. And we have to face the fact that my client has been incarcerated for almost 30 months. And despite the risk that is entailed in the fact that the documents may not be found, we are ready to go on trial. And this is as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina documents are concerned. As far as the documents from Croatia are concerned, irrespective of the fact that the correspondence has been confidential, there's no reason for us to go into private session because the Defence does not have anything to add to what has been submitted in writing on several occasions. The last submission dates 5 April 2004. If we try and summarise the situation as it is at the moment, we have to say that the Government of the Republic of Croatia has placed at the disposal of the Defence the majority of the requested documents, that we are still requesting a number of them, a number which is not insignificant. And it remains to be seen whether we are going to be able to locate these documents in the rich archives of the Government of the Republic of Croatia. In any case, this and other pending issues that have been mentioned in our written submissions, the Defence is going to inform the Trial Chamber about those as soon as possible. And we do not want to use problems with the Government of the Republic of Croatia as an excuse for the rescheduling of the beginning of trial. The Defence is not going to ask for a delay because of the fact that we are still requesting a number of documents from the Government of the Republic of Croatia. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are absolutely certain that you possess very high professional qualities, and I'm very happy to hear your interpretation of the -- that has given me some concern. If I understand you well, the majority of documents have been provided to you. I would like to ask Mr. Harmon now: Does the Prosecution have in their custody documents that were obtained from the archives of the Government of Croatia? If I understand well, you have carried out a search, and you do have access to the archives of the Government of Croatia. You have even told us how many days you worked in those archives. I don't know whether what you have in terms of the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina is available to you in terms of the archives of the Government of Croatia. Are there any documents that might be of use to the Defence and that might enable them to prepare their case? Do you have any such documents in your custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we both have equal access to the archives in Croatia. So we have gone, as you quite accurately note, we have somebody who has gone down there and looked in those archives, and that search has yielded certain documents to us. The Defence has done the same. Whatever documents that we have that may assist the Defence under Rule 68 we have given to the Defence. The rest of the documents are documents that we have retained. The Defence of this case is not spelled out, so it's up to guesswork to determine what the actual Defence is. We have given them what we are required to give under law and the rules and procedure of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your position. However, I also believe, and I hope you will agree with me, that according to Article 68, there may be different interpretations, rather broad even, so I would like to invite you and I would like to appeal to your professionalism and to our common desire to arrive at the truth to address this issue as quickly as possible. I would like to -- you to throw a second glance at those documents and see whether you have some documents in your possession that are -- have been requested by the Defence, that the Article 68 doesn't cover. It's going to help us on our way to arriving at the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My first comment, Your Honour, is for those of us who have worked with Rule 68 for a long time, it's harder for -- it's hard for me to imagine a more broadly drafted rule than Rule 68 until its most recent amendment. It's very difficult, and often times, and indeed in this case, I have invited the Defence to provide me with one of two things, provide me with the general nature of the defence, in which case I can focus my search and I can identify documents that may apply to those that the Defence, in its general contours, they can get the documents sooner to assist them. Alternatively, if there are specific items they are identify with precision, we can look for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the interruption. Are these documents that you have requested from the Government of Croatia, are you a hundred per cent sure, a hundred per cent sure that these documents are not in your possession, the documents that have been requested from the Government of Croatia that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't say with a hundred per cent certainty what you've asked me. I can meet with the Defence. The Defence can give me a very precise list of documents. We can go back through our archives and look for those documents. And that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you. I believe that in this spirit of cooperation, light will be shed on that issue. I also believe that I don't need to remind you that you can always count on Mr. Harhoff for his cooperation. He is really a very dedicated person. I would also like to say that I'm glad that the Prosecution has confirmed what I have in front of me, and that is that the Prosecution is going to call 53 witnesses, 40 of them in person, viva voce, and that the Prosecution estimates that they will need 127 hours for their examination-in-chief of these witnesses. Is this information correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is almost correct. I can tell you that we have not remained idle. When this submission was made to Your Honours, it was a considerable period of time ago. In the meantime, we have filed with the Court two motions identifying -- notification regarding additional witnesses. In addition to that, I have identified two more potential witnesses. So our list is somewhat flexible in the sense of its numbers. I haven't sat down and tried to eliminate some witnesses for the addition of other witnesses, and I'm continuing to make assessments on information that I get, and very good information that I get. And I am pursuing that personally. And I will inform the Court when the Court -- I think at an appropriate time when some additional decisions are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your diplomatic language. You're saying that the list is very flexible. However, this flexibility sometimes may go too far. Please, stay within the limits. You may replace one witness by another, and these are the limits that will be acceptable. And if I understand you well, we are still talking about 127 hours of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My figures were slightly different. I had 136 hours of examination-in-chief. But it's not a great difference, and we can sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. An approximate date, a rough date that has been suggested by -- yes, Mr. Harmon, you wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I think I can account for the -- I believe I can account for the difference between 127 and 136, and that is that I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: It is to be accurate, it's 127 and half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We then filed a notification regarding additional witness, and time was added to those witnesses, and those subtractions were made from the original for you. But we can make those adjustments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you. So if I understand correctly, Mr. Harhoff is proposing that the parties be ready to start right before, or rather in the first days of July. I think that this has been agreed upon by the parties as well. The last question that I need to look at concerns the health of Mr. Ljubicic. So, Mr. Ljubicic, would you prefer to go -- for us to go into private session or you don't think it will be necessary? It's really up to you to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think it is necessary for this session to be closed or private. As for my health, it is very good for the time being. I do not experience any problems or difficulties in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad to hear that. Thank you very much. You may sit down, Mr. Ljubicic. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is. I'm just -- have a query as to what you just said, and that is that the parties should be ready to start in the first days of July. Obviously, I take it Your Honour is referring to starting trial in the first days of July, and any direction that we are given we will abide by. But I'm currently in another trial, as Your Honour knows. And the question I have is: There's a lot of preparation that is required to get ready for a trial in July. And I'm prepared to do that, without any reservation. But if it is an empty exercise or an empty gesture that's going to affect other work that I do and my colleagues do. So if -- what I would respectfully request from Your Honour is if this is a firm date, then I would be satisfied to have it announced. If it is not a firm date, then I would also request some clarification on it because I have to set things in motion in order to get witnesses here, start those arrangements. And it's a very, very difficult thing to start and then disengage from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. I do understand your position. But I also understand the position of the Defence. It is true Mr. Ljubicic has now spent quite some time in detention. As for the date, it is not a fixed date. It is not a final date. For the time being, it is merely a proposal that I offer to you. Because after all, parties have to agree on that, and there are still pending issues. I am aware of that. And that the Defence would like, and justly so, to verify. So with the help of Mr. Harhoff, I think it will perhaps be more useful if you could propose, if you could suggest a date. But I hope you're not going to wait for other cases to be finished. Because it seems to me that the case you are currently engaged in is likely to take some time. So I hope that we will be able to come up finally with a solution that will enable the Defence to get ready and also for you to prepare your case. So to answer your question, the date, when I said the first days of July, is only an approximative date. It's not a fixed or a final date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Anything else, Mr. Jonjic? Thank you. Well, let me just wish you a lot of success in your future work. Let me also thank the interpreters. The hearing is closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: at 3.45 p.m.
